query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, increasing the relative amounts of Al and Cr while reducing the relative mobility (or effective concentration) of Mn leads to a preferential outward diffusion of Al and Cr during high-temperature exposure (above 900 °C). This promotes the formation of a continuous, coherent, and adherent protective oxide layer comprised primarily of Al2O3 and Cr2O3, whereas alloys with higher Mn content/mobility develop predominantly Mn-rich oxides that are unstable and prone to cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX HEAs (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state with a baseline composition containing standard Mn levels.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloying element ratios to increase the Al and Cr content relative to Mn (or control Mn mobility), thereby favoring the diffusion of protective elements to the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres (e.g., in air with sufficient oxygen partial pressure) for prolonged durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a duplex oxide scale where an inner Cr2O3-rich layer and an outer Al2O3-rich layer provide a coherent and adherent barrier against further oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced Al and Cr content promotes their preferential diffusion to the surface where they form slow-growing, protective oxides. Simultaneously, suppressing Mn mobility minimizes the formation of fast-growing, unstable Mn-oxides that can lead to cracking or spallation. This leverages principles observed in Ti–Al intermetallic systems to control diffusion kinetics and oxide formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy with higher Al/Cr and lower effective Mn will develop a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide layer that resists cracking and spallation under high-temperature oxidative conditions.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiX HEAs with standard (or relatively higher) Mn content and lower relative Al and Cr concentrations, where oxidation results in the formation of thicker, more heterogeneous, and unstable oxide scales dominated by Mn-rich phases.
generation.boundary: Applicable to high-temperature (above 900 °C) exposure in oxidative or corrosive environments; the hypothesis assumes similar processing conditions that result in comparable microstructural states in single- or multiphase solid solutions.
generation.uncertainty: While the approach builds on insights from Ti–Al systems, the exact diffusion kinetics and phase stability in complex HEAs may deviate from simpler intermetallic analogues. Variability in processing, phase formation, or unexpected intermetallic compounds could affect the oxidation behavior and scale properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of CrFeCoNiX HEA samples: one with the modified composition (higher Al/Cr and reduced Mn mobility) and one baseline sample with standard composition. Expose both sample sets to temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air) for identical durations. Characterize the oxide scales formed using cross-sectional SEM, EDS for elemental mapping, and XRD for phase identification.
measurements: Oxide composition and phase distribution (especially ratios of Al2O3, Cr2O3, and Mn-oxides)
Coherency and adhesion of the oxide layer (crack density, spallation occurrence)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloys do not consistently exhibit a thinner, more continuous, and adherent oxide scale with dominant Al2O3 and Cr2O3 phases and reduced evidence of unstable, Mn-rich oxide formation, compared to the baseline alloys, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA was successfully fabricated through the arc-melting process, with an emphasis on phase, microstructure, and real-time oxidation behaviour in two different non-ambient (high-temperature and low-oxygen partial pressure) conditions. The main findings of this research work can be summarised as follows. In a vacuum (4.2 × 10−6 atm), only MnO, a halite-type oxide, was formed during in situ oxidation, contrary to ThermoCalc’s prediction of both halite and spinel oxides, and Ni/Co forming halite. In air (1.0 atm), vigorous oxidation was observed, with most of the oxides formed being spinel. Mn remained important in the formation of spinel oxides, and Co was predicted to form spinel oxides by ThermoCalc but was not found in oxide-forming elements. Oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, and Fe3O4 were not detected during in situ HTXRD in either vacuum or air, which contrasts with previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. Mn was found to be a higher oxide-forming element, producing non-protective oxides, and leading to the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy beneath the oxide layer. The following was found:Under HVOF spraying, the processes of oxidation and phase transformations occur in the following sequence: (i) pronounced Al diffusion from subsurface BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface; (ii) particle’s surface Al2O3 formation; and (iii) FCC formation in the Al-depleted subsurface layer.During continuous heating in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) Al diffusion to the surface; and (iii) simultaneous formation of Al2O3 and FCC due to Al outflow from BCC/B2.During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) diffusion of Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo to the surface; and (iii) formation of surface Al2O3 and undersurface sigma due to enrichment of the undersurface zone with Cr

At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. The presence of Mn, known for its high mobility and low-energy oxide formation, can deplete Mn in the alloy, causing pore formation and accelerating oxide growth. Tradition

reading.lever: Adjust alloying element ratios to enhance Al/Cr diffusion while suppressing Mn mobility for coherent protective oxide formation.
reading.why: This approach leverages insights from Ti–Al intermetallics, promising a direct mitigation of Mn-induced spallation in CrFeCoNiX HEAs.
